blocks.text: Give clients a single entry point that authenticates, routes and aggregates calls to the services behind it.

Instead of every client knowing every service address, protocol and auth scheme, a **gateway** terminates the request at the edge. It applies cross-cutting policy once, routes by path or header, and can compose several backend calls into one response tailored to a client type.

items: **Routing:** path, host or header to a service.
**Policy at the edge:** authentication, rate limits, TLS, logging.
**Composition:** one client call fans out to several services.
**Translation:** public REST to internal gRPC, or mobile to desktop payloads.

blocks.text: The gateway is on every request path. It must stay thin and highly available, or it becomes a bottleneck and a distributed monolith's front door.

cards.expectedOutput:
/users/7 -> 200 user:7
/home -> 200 user:7 | orders:2
/orders/7 -> 401 unauthorized
/billing -> 404 no route

walkthrough.note: The gateway owns the route table (longest prefix wins) and the auth check. Unauthenticated requests are rejected before any service sees them; unknown paths get a 404.
`/home` is composed: both calls run concurrently. The optional orders call has a timeout and a fallback, so it degrades to a placeholder instead of failing the page.
Services are registered behind prefixes. They are lambdas here; in production they are remote clients with their own timeouts.
The client sees one address. A valid token reaches services and composes; a bad token or unknown path never leaves the gateway.

blocks.text: A mobile banking app on twelve backend services.

The home screen needs balance, recent transactions and offers. Calling three services over a cellular link costs three round trips and exposes internal topology. A gateway offers `GET /mobile/home`: it validates the JWT once, calls the services in parallel with a 300 ms budget, drops the optional offers on timeout and returns one compact payload. The web client gets its own, different composition.
Payoff: one round trip for the app, one place for auth and rate limits, and services stay free to be split or renamed behind the facade.

lists.title: Use when
items: Many clients need one stable, secured address for many services.
Cross-cutting policy (auth, quotas, TLS) belongs at the edge.
Different client types need differently shaped responses.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: There is one service and one client: a plain reverse proxy is enough.
Services call each other: east-west traffic belongs to a mesh, not the edge gateway.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Business logic creeping into the gateway until every team must change it.
A single shared gateway owned by one team becomes a release bottleneck.
Aggregation without timeouts and fallbacks makes the slowest service your latency.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Gateway routes that rewrite payloads field by field for each service.
A gateway in front of a monolith that only forwards requests.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Virtual threads and `CompletableFuture` make fan-out composition short; set a deadline on each call.
Java 21 records make good immutable request and response envelopes at the gateway boundary.

rows.difference: A facade simplifies an in-process subsystem. A gateway is a networked facade that also enforces security, quotas and protocol translation for remote clients.
A proxy stands in for one object with the same interface. A gateway exposes a different, client-oriented API over many services.
A gateway is a shared north-south entry point at the edge. A sidecar is per-instance and handles that service's own traffic, including service-to-service calls.
The gateway is the routing facade a strangler migration needs: paths move from legacy to new services without clients noticing.
Quotas and throttling are typically enforced at the gateway, per client or API key, before traffic reaches services.

options.why: One entry point authenticates, throttles and routes requests to several backend services.
A facade simplifies a local subsystem; it does not enforce auth and quotas for remote clients.
The checks here are fixed sequential code, not pluggable handlers deciding whether to pass the request on.
The switch picks a destination by path; there is no interchangeable algorithm behind one interface.

exercises.scenario: A mobile app renders its home screen from five microservices, so it makes five calls on a slow network. Security wants a single place to validate tokens, and the service topology is changing every quarter.

options.why: One edge entry point validates tokens once, composes the five calls into one, and hides the changing topology.
A sidecar handles each service's own traffic; it does not give the client one composed endpoint.
An ambassador helps a client reach one remote resource; it does not compose or secure many services for external callers.
Adapting one interface to another does not aggregate calls or centralize authentication.

exercises.prompt: Explain an API Gateway: what it centralizes, what it should not do, and how it differs from a sidecar.

modelAnswer.text: A gateway is the single edge entry point that authenticates, rate-limits, routes and composes calls to backend services, so clients stay simple. It should stay thin: routing and policy, not business logic. A sidecar sits beside each service instance and handles its own traffic, including service-to-service calls.

keyPoints: One entry point for routing, auth, quotas and TLS
Can compose several backend calls into one response
Keep it thin: no business logic, with timeouts and fallbacks
It is a shared north-south hop, a bottleneck risk
A sidecar is per instance; the gateway is shared at the edge
